strengths: AugSub provides a simple, technically coherent way to combine supervised learning with self-distillation from a less regularized pass to a more regularized pass of the same network. It accommodates dropout, stochastic depth, and masking without adding inference cost or a separate teacher. Its supported practical contribution favors weak acceptance.

The core ImageNet results are convincing. Table 3 reports improvements of 0.6–0.7 percentage points across ViT-S through ViT-H at 400 epochs, with gains persisting at 800 epochs. Table A.2 reports ViT-B accuracy of 84.08 ± 0.02 versus the baseline's 83.46 ± 0.04, supporting the reliability of this improvement.

The paper meaningfully accounts for training cost. In Table 6, ViT-B with AugMask achieves 84.1% using 25 GPU days versus 83.7% using 26 GPU days for longer baseline training. MAE ViT-L fine-tuning improves from 85.5% to 86.1% at the same reported cost.

Evaluation covers multiple architectures and training recipes, robustness benchmarks, and downstream tasks. Examples include ImageNet-A improvement from 51.9% to 58.3% for ViT-H and ADE20k gains of 0.4–0.6 mIoU. Using a fixed 50% masking ratio across these recipes strengthens the evidence for practical applicability.

The equations, concise pseudocode, and detailed training configurations in Appendix B make the method understandable and support reproducibility. Selected experiments include three-run statistics, and the manuscript supplies a code URL.
weaknesses: Originality relative to closely related methods remains insufficiently established. Section 2 acknowledges Co-sub and self-distillation, but there is no direct experimental comparison with Co-sub or a closely matched consistency-regularization method. The results establish improvements over standard recipes more clearly than the distinct contribution over existing sub-model training objectives.

The ablations do not isolate the central benefit of relaxed supervision. Table 1 compares a single regularized supervised pass against an approach that also retains a fully supervised, less regularized pass. A control averaging Equations 1 and 2 would distinguish the contribution of soft targets from that of retaining ordinary supervision alongside the regularized branch. The roles of asymmetric supervision and stop-gradient are also not tested.

The adaptive-difficulty explanation is stronger than the evidence. Equation 3 penalizes prediction disagreement and does not restrict regularization to correctly classified examples, contrary to the 'exclusively' successful-example description in Section 3.1. Figure 3's aggregate gradient norms do not establish this sample-level mechanism. This is a limitation of the interpretation rather than a demonstrated failure of the objective.

Benefits have meaningful boundaries. Adding AugMask during fine-tuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.9% to 89.6% in Table 10, and Section 4.2 states that CLIP's best-checkpoint performance is unchanged. Hierarchical models also require approximately twice the training computation; the favorable ViT budget comparisons do not establish equivalent efficiency across all architectures.

Statistical support is uneven for the smaller improvements. The 0.1-point BEiT v2 and Swin-T gains and the 0.2–0.3 AP COCO gains lack reported variability. Some transfer gains are small relative to the reported variation—for example, ViT-S Flowers improves from 94.54 ± 1.71 to 95.19 ± 1.95 with AugMask pretraining. Claims of consistently significant improvement should therefore be qualified.
